This was from Grok:

What kind of impact would a plane the size of a new Lear jet make on a paved road with an impact at about almost straight down at 300+ miles an hour? and what actual debris would be left????

Answer:

That impact is in the range of a small bomb. A Learjet seventy-five weighs around twenty-one thousand pounds, so at three hundred miles per hour you’ve got roughly eighty-seven megajoules of kinetic energy — about twenty kilograms of TNT. 

The airframe wouldn’t survive as a recognizable shape. You’d get a crater maybe ten to fifteen feet across and several feet deep, with the engines likely punching through the pavement or detonating on contact. The wings shear off instantly, and with over a thousand gallons of jet fuel on board, you’d have a fireball that engulfs the whole scene before the debris even stops moving.
What remains is a debris field — twisted aluminum skin panels, composite fragments, landing gear struts bent like paperclips, engine cores that may stay partially intact because they’re the densest part. Glass from the cockpit would be pulverized into fine grit mixed with the crater rubble. No intact seats, no recognizable cabin. It’s the same physics that turned Flight ninety-three’s wreckage into a scorched circle in a Pennsylvania field.

One thing worth noting — real aircraft almost never hit straight down at terminal velocity because they break up or catch air on the way. The closest real-world analog is probably the nineteen ninety-four USAir crash in Pittsburgh, where a seven thirty-seven hit at a steep angle and left a crater with a debris field stretching hundreds of yards.
